title: Loops
summary: A loop repeats a group of steps. It can count through numbers or visit every item in a list.
introduction: A loop repeats a group of steps. It can count through numbers or visit every item in a list. Imagine handing one pencil to each student. Write the hand-out step once, then let a loop repeat it for the whole list.
learningObjectives: Write a counting loop with for and an open-ended loop with while
Iterate over arrays and strings with for...of and over object keys with for...in
Skip or stop iterations with continue and break
Recognise and fix an infinite loop

blocks.text: A `for` loop has three parts in its parentheses, separated by semicolons: an **initialiser** that runs once (`let i = 1`), a **condition** checked before every pass (`i <= 5`), and an **update** that runs after every pass (`i++`). Use it when you know how many times to repeat, or when you need the counter itself.

The counter is declared with `let` because it changes, and because `let` is block-scoped each pass gets its own `i`. Counting from `0` is the norm when the counter is used as an array index, since array positions start at zero.

`while` repeats as long as its condition is true, which suits problems where the number of passes is unknown: keep compounding interest until the balance reaches a target, keep asking until the input is valid. `do...while` is the same, except the block runs once *before* the condition is checked, so it always executes at least one time.

blocks.title: The infinite loop
blocks.text: If the condition never becomes false the loop never ends and the page freezes. The usual cause is forgetting the update: `while (balance < 150) { years++; }` never changes `balance`. Before running a `while` loop, check that something inside the block moves the condition towards false. If a page does freeze, close the tab; on this site the output panel reports a run that has not finished within ten seconds.

Most loops in real code visit every element of an array, and `for...of` does exactly that without a counter. It also works on strings (one character at a time) and on other iterable values such as `Map` and `Set`. When you need the index as well, loop over `array.entries()`, which yields `[index, element]` pairs.

blocks.text: for...in: the keys of an object

`for...in` visits the property names of an object. Use the key in square brackets to read the matching value. Do not use `for...in` on arrays: it gives you index strings rather than elements and may include extra properties. For arrays, use `for...of`.

`continue` skips the rest of the current pass and moves on to the next one; `break` leaves the loop entirely. Both work in every loop type. They are the clean way to express 'ignore these items' and 'stop as soon as we have found it'.

A loop inside a loop runs the inner one completely for every pass of the outer one. That is how you handle grids, tables and combinations. Keep the nesting shallow: two levels are common, three are a sign that part of the work belongs in a function.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Print the numbers from 10 down to 1 with a `for` loop, then print every third letter of `"abcdefghij"` using `continue`. Finish by converting the balance example into a `do...while` loop and checking that the output stays the same.

questions.question: How many times does the body of `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)` run?
questions.explanation: i takes the values 0, 1 and 2; when it reaches 3 the condition i < 3 is false and the loop stops. That is three passes.

questions.question: `for...in` is the recommended loop for visiting the elements of an array.
questions.explanation: for...in iterates over property names (index strings) and is meant for objects. Use for...of for array elements.
